synonyms: ["Pruritis Associated With Aids", "Itching Associated With AIDS Or HIV", "Itching Related To AIDS Or HIV", "Itchy Skin Caused By AIDS Or HIV"]
conventional_description: Conventional medicine understands HIV-associated pruritus as a common and often distressing symptom. It can stem from several causes: the direct effect of HIV on the immune system, opportunistic skin infections, medication side effects, dry skin (xerosis), or systemic conditions like kidney or liver dysfunction that are more common in people living with HIV. Diagnosis usually involves a physical exam, a review of current medications, and sometimes blood tests or a skin biopsy to rule out infections or other dermatological conditions. Treatment is typically aimed at the presumed cause - antihistamines for allergic reactions, antifungals or antibiotics for infections, and emollients for dry skin - but often the itch persists despite these measures.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment typically begins with topical emollients and oral antihistamines. If a specific skin infection is identified, antifungal, antibacterial, or antiviral creams or pills are prescribed. For more severe or persistent cases, doctors may use corticosteroids, either topical or systemic. When pruritus is linked to a specific medication, adjusting the antiretroviral regimen is considered. Phototherapy is sometimes used for widespread itching that does not respond to other treatments.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands pruritus in HIV as a sign of deeper internal disharmony, most often involving the Blood, the Spleen, and the Liver.
The skin is seen as an extension of the body's internal environment - when the Blood is deficient, the skin becomes dry and undernourished, leading to a fine, shifting itch. When the Spleen is too weak to transform fluids, Dampness accumulates and can combine with Heat to create red, oozing, burning eruptions. The Liver, which governs the smooth flow of Qi and stores the Blood, is also central: emotional stress or long-term illness can cause Liver Qi to stagnate, generating internal Wind that manifests as an unpredictable, moving itch.
In HIV, the underlying Wei Qi (defensive Qi) is often compromised, making the skin more vulnerable to external pathogens like Wind-Heat, which can trigger sudden, red, itchy wheals. This is why the same diagnosis of HIV-associated pruritus can present so differently from person to person - the skin is a mirror reflecting a unique combination of deficiencies (Blood, Qi, Yin) and excesses (Dampness, Heat, Wind).
This is why TCM practitioners pay close attention to the quality of the itch: a dry, night-time itch with pale skin points to Blood Deficiency; a persistent, low-grade itch with crushing fatigue suggests Qi and Blood Deficiency; an intermittent itch with thirst and night sweats indicates Qi and Yin Deficiency; and a burning, red, oozing rash points to Damp-Heat. Each pattern has its own distinct tongue and pulse presentation, and each requires a different treatment strategy.
classical_quote: 「风瘙痒者，由血虚风邪乘之，搏于皮肤，与气血相击，故痒也。」
classical_translation: "Wind-itch occurs when blood is deficient and wind evil takes advantage of this, attacking the skin and clashing with qi and blood, thereby causing itching."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Causes and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Chapter on Wind-Itch (风瘙痒) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by looking at the skin itself and asking about the timing and quality of the itch. Dry, flaky skin that worsens at night points toward Blood Deficiency with External Wind, whereas red, oozing, burning eruptions suggest Damp-Heat. The tongue and pulse are then checked to confirm the underlying pattern.
When the skin is very dry, pale, and scaly, with a pale tongue and a thin or wiry-thready pulse, the root is Blood Deficiency failing to nourish the skin, allowing external Wind to invade. The itch is often worse at night and improves with moisturizing. Dizziness and a pale face may accompany it.
If the itch is persistent but low-grade, and the person feels profoundly tired with a pale complexion, the picture is Qi and Blood Deficiency. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse is weak or thready. The skin may be slightly dry but not as scaly as in pure Blood Deficiency with Wind.
An intermittent itch with dry mouth, thirst, and poor appetite, alongside a pale tongue with little coating, indicates Qi and Yin Deficiency. This pattern often arises from long-term illness or medication use. The pulse is thready and may be rapid or weak, reflecting the dual depletion of energy and fluids.
Red, moist, or weeping lesions that feel hot and burn intensely signal Damp-Heat. The tongue is red with a thick, greasy yellow coat, and the pulse is slippery and rapid. This pattern is more inflammatory and acute-feeling than the deficiency patterns, and the itch is often accompanied by a heavy sensation.
Purplish, dark, or stubbornly thickened plaques that itch with a stabbing pain suggest Blood Stagnation. The tongue may be dark with purple spots, and the pulse choppy or wiry. This type of itch resists simple anti-itch remedies and is more common in advanced or chronic cases.
A sudden outbreak of red wheals that appear quickly, often after a new drug or infection, points to an acute Wind-Heat invasion. The tongue is red with a thin yellow coat, and the pulse is floating and rapid. The itch is intense but tends to come and go more abruptly than the chronic patterns.

patterns.symptoms: ["Itching that shifts location and comes and goes", "Dry, flaky, or rough skin", "Worse at night", "Aversion to wind or drafts", "Pale or sallow complexion", "Dizziness or light-headedness"]
patterns.worse_with: Exposure to wind or drafts, Dry environment, Nighttime, Spicy, fried, or drying foods, Overwork or overexertion, Blood loss (e.g., heavy menses)
patterns.better_with: Moisturising the skin, Eating blood-nourishing foods, Gentle movement, such as Tai Chi or walking, Avoiding drafts, Warmth and adequate rest
patterns.why_this_happens: Chronic HIV gradually depletes the body's Blood, leaving the skin undernourished and dry. This dryness generates internal Wind, and because the surface is weak, external Wind easily invades. The result is a shifting, parched itch that worsens at night and feels worse in drafts.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with a thin white and slightly dry coating. Pulse: fine (thin) overall, wiry at the left middle position (Liver), and often floating at the right front position (Lung/Exterior).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Deficiency leaves skin dry and defenceless, so wind and dryness easily provoke itching. Nighttime is Yin time, and Blood belongs to Yin, so the deficiency is felt most then. Overwork and blood loss further deplete Blood. Nourishing foods and moisturising replenish Blood and Yin, while avoiding drafts and resting protect the surface. Gentle movement circulates Blood without draining it, helping to calm the internal Wind.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat blood-nourishing foods like dark leafy greens, bone broth, eggs, and moderate amounts of red meat. Avoid drying, spicy, or fried foods and limit alcohol. Keep skin well-moisturised and protect it from wind and drafts. Gentle daily movement like Tai Chi or walking helps Blood flow without exhausting your reserves.

patterns.why_this_happens: HIV gradually depletes the body's Qi and Blood, the fundamental substances that nourish and moisten every tissue. When the Spleen cannot produce enough Qi and Blood, the skin loses its nourishment, becoming dry, pale, and papery. Without sufficient Blood to anchor the mind, the persistent low-grade itch is often accompanied by fatigue, dizziness, and a sallow complexion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin, with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine and weak (细弱, xì ruò), lacking force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are produced by the Spleen from the food we eat. Warm, cooked foods and rest make this production efficient, while raw, cold foods and overwork put out the digestive fire. The itch subsides when the skin is finally moistened by newly generated Blood; moxibustion and acupuncture on ST-36 and SP-6 directly stimulate this generation process, while stress and exhaustion burn through Qi faster than the body can replenish it.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warm, easily digestible, and nourishing foods like bone broths, congees with goji berries and red dates, and gently cooked dark leafy greens. Avoid raw, cold foods and overwork; gentle walking and regular rest are better than intense exercise, which can further deplete Qi.

patterns.why_this_happens: Chronic HIV infection and the long-term use of medications gradually deplete the body's Qi (vital energy) and Yin (cooling, moistening fluids). When Qi is too weak to nourish the skin and Yin fluids run dry, the skin loses its natural moisture and becomes under-nourished, leading to a dry, intermittent itch. The mild Empty Heat that arises from Yin deficiency can also cause night sweats and a subtle warm sensation, making the itch more noticeable when the body is at rest.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale-red or pale body with a thin or absent coating, possibly cracked and dry. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, may be slightly rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Yin are like the body's fuel and coolant. Overwork, stress, and lack of sleep burn through them, leaving the skin dry and itchy. Spicy and fried foods add heat that consumes Yin, making the itch worse. Rest, moistening foods, and gentle activity help replenish Qi and Yin, cooling the mild empty heat and restoring the skin's nourishment.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, frequent, easily digested meals like congee, soups, and steamed vegetables. Include moistening foods such as pears, honey, and lily bulb. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods that consume Yin. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork; gentle practices like Tai Chi or Qi Gong can help conserve Qi.

patterns.worse_with: Hot, humid weather, Greasy, spicy, or fried foods, Alcohol, Stress and frustration, Sedentary lifestyle
patterns.better_with: Cool, dry weather, Light, non-greasy meals, Cooling foods (cucumber, mung beans), Gentle movement, such as Tai Chi or walking
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body fails to transform fluids properly, Dampness accumulates and combines with Heat-often from medications, secondary infections, or a rich, greasy diet. This Damp-Heat stews internally and then erupts outward into the skin, creating red, oozing, burning lesions that itch intensely. The sticky, heavy nature of Dampness makes the itching cling and worsen in humid conditions, while the Heat adds redness and a prickling sensation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow, greasy coating that is thickest in the centre and root, may be swollen with teeth marks. Pulse: soggy-rapid (Ru Shu) or slippery-rapid (Hua Shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Dampness and Heat are both heavy, sticky pathogens that thrive in humid, hot conditions and are fed by rich, greasy foods and alcohol. Such triggers literally add more Dampness and Heat to the body, making the skin eruptions angrier and itchier. Cooling, drying foods and a dry environment help counteract that internal stew. Stress stirs up Liver Qi, which can transform into Heat and worsen the pattern, while gentle movement keeps Qi and fluids moving so they don't stagnate into Dampness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and sugary foods, as well as alcohol and dairy, which all generate Dampness and Heat. Favour cooling, light foods like cucumber, mung beans, celery, and barley. Keep living spaces cool and dry, and wear loose, breathable cotton clothing. Gentle daily movement like walking or qi gong helps circulate Qi and drain Dampness, but avoid exercising in hot, humid weather.

patterns.why_this_happens: In chronic HIV, long-term illness and Qi deficiency slow the circulation of Blood. When Blood flow becomes sluggish or stuck, it fails to nourish the skin, leading to dryness and roughness. The stagnant Blood itself generates micro-obstructions and local heat, which manifests as a deep, stubborn itch that feels fixed and stabbing rather than diffuse. Lesions often appear purplish or dusky, reflecting the underlying stasis.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body with stasis spots; distended dark sublingual veins; thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 Sè) like a knife scraping bamboo, or wiry (弦 Xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and inactivity cause Blood to congeal like a frozen stream, making stasis worse. Warmth, gentle movement, and blood-moving foods restore circulation, so the skin receives proper nourishment and the stagnant heat that drives the itch can dissipate. Stress knots the Liver Qi, which is the main force pushing Blood through the vessels; keeping the mind calm and the Qi smooth directly loosens the grip of stasis on the skin.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, blood-moving foods like turmeric, ginger, black vinegar, and a little red meat or bone broth. Gentle daily movement-walking, stretching, or tai chi-keeps Blood flowing. Avoid cold drinks and raw foods, which congeal circulation. Manage stress with breathing or quiet time, as emotional strain tightens the Liver Qi and worsens stasis.

patterns.why_this_happens: When external Wind-Heat invades the body, it clashes with the defensive Qi at the skin's surface. The Heat inflames the skin, causing red, raised wheals and an intense, sudden itch. In HIV, the immune system is already weakened, making it harder to fight off these external attacks. This acute flare is often triggered by a new allergen, a medication reaction, or an infection, and it typically brings systemic signs like a sore throat and mild fever.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red tip and edges, thin yellow coating. Pulse: floating and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat is an external pathogen that inflames the skin. Spicy foods, alcohol, and hot environments add more Heat, while wind exposure strengthens the invading Wind. Cooling foods, rest, and avoiding triggers help the body expel the pathogen and calm the skin. The acupuncture points and herbs work by dispersing Wind and clearing Heat from the surface, directly addressing the root of the acute itch.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Drink cooling teas like chrysanthemum or mint. Avoid spicy, greasy, and allergenic foods. Keep the skin cool with loose clothing and avoid hot showers. Gentle exercise like walking helps the defensive Qi, but avoid sweating heavily. Do not scratch; use a cold compress instead.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure my HIV-associated itching?
faqs.answer: TCM can be very effective at managing and significantly reducing HIV-associated pruritus, but it is not a cure for the underlying HIV infection. The goal of TCM treatment is to correct the internal imbalances that cause the itch - whether that's nourishing deficient Blood, clearing Damp-Heat, or expelling Wind. Many patients find their itching resolves completely or becomes much milder, and this improvement can be long-lasting when the underlying pattern is addressed. However, because HIV is a chronic condition that can shift over time, occasional maintenance treatments may be needed.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs with my HIV medications?
faqs.answer: Safety is the top priority. Many herbs can be used safely alongside antiretroviral therapy (ART), but there are known interactions with certain plants, particularly St. John's Wort, which can reduce the effectiveness of some HIV drugs. Always bring your complete medication list to your TCM practitioner, and inform your HIV doctor you are considering or using herbal medicine. A qualified TCM practitioner will select formulas that support your health without interfering with your life-saving medications. Never stop or adjust your ART without consulting your prescribing doctor.

faqs.question: Will acupuncture make my itching worse?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture is generally very safe and should not worsen your itching. In fact, many patients feel a soothing, cooling sensation during treatment for Damp-Heat or Wind-Heat patterns. Your practitioner will use points that calm the mind, clear heat, and stop itch. The needles are hair-thin and single-use, so infection risk is not a concern. If you have a very low platelet count, tell your practitioner so they can use gentler needle techniques.

faqs.question: How many acupuncture sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: For acute flare-ups of itching, one or two sessions a week for 2-4 weeks is a common starting point. For chronic, long-standing pruritus, especially from deficiency patterns, weekly sessions for 8-12 weeks are more typical. Your practitioner will track your progress and taper the frequency as your skin improves. Many patients transition to a maintenance schedule of once a month or once every other month once the itching is under control.

faqs.question: What dietary changes can help my itching?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a key role in TCM because food directly influences the body's internal environment. Generally, avoid foods that create Dampness and Heat, such as fried foods, alcohol, spicy dishes, and excessive sugar. Focus on easily digestible, nourishing foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and soups. If your skin is dry and scaly, add blood-nourishing foods like dark leafy greens, small amounts of organ meats, and black sesame seeds. If your rash is red and oozing, cooling foods like cucumber, mung beans, and watermelon are very helpful. Your TCM practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside antihistamines or steroid creams?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM is often used alongside conventional treatments. Many patients begin TCM while still using their prescribed antihistamines or topical steroids. As the underlying imbalance improves and the itching subsides, you can work with your doctor to safely reduce or taper these medications. Do not stop any prescribed medication abruptly without your doctor's supervision. Herbs with sedative properties should be used carefully with antihistamines to avoid excessive drowsiness.

research.title: 艾滋病皮肤瘙痒协同治疗专家共识
research.description: This expert consensus document provides comprehensive guidance on the TCM pattern differentiation and treatment of skin itching in HIV/AIDS patients. It outlines the main patterns - including Blood Deficiency with Wind, Damp-Heat, and Qi and Yin Deficiency - and recommends specific herbal formulas, acupoints, and lifestyle modifications. The consensus is based on the clinical experience of a panel of TCM and HIV specialists in China.

research.title: 中医药治疗艾滋病30年回顾与展望
research.description: This 30-year review of TCM treatment for AIDS summarizes the evolution of pattern differentiation and herbal therapy for common HIV-related symptoms, including pruritus. It highlights the shift toward integrated care and the growing recognition of TCM's role in managing chronic symptoms and improving quality of life. The review discusses key formulas used for skin manifestations and their underlying rationale.

research.title: 1266例HIV/AIDS患者中医临床症状体征分布规律分析
research.description: This cross-sectional study analyzed the distribution of TCM symptoms and signs in 1,266 HIV/AIDS patients. It found that skin itching is a common complaint and identified the most frequent accompanying patterns, including Qi and Blood Deficiency, Damp-Heat, and Yin Deficiency. The study provides epidemiological support for the TCM patterns seen in clinical practice.
